title: 'Remembrance': Gondal origin and publication
short: Written in March 1845 as a Gondal poem headed 'R. Alcona to J. Brenzaida', and published as 'Remembrance' in Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell (1846).
body: Emily and Anne Brontë invented the imaginary island kingdom of Gondal in childhood and continued to write its saga into adulthood. In the manuscript, the poem is spoken by Rosina Alcona, mourning Julius Brenzaida, emperor of Gondal, who had died fifteen years before. For publication in 1846 (the sisters' collection that famously sold two copies) Emily removed the names and retitled it, so that it reads as a poem of personal bereavement. Since the poem was written in the voice of a fictional character, biographical readings must be cautious.

anchor: the deep snow piled above thee
title: Metre and rhyme
short: Long lines of about five stresses rhyme abab; the first and third lines often end in feminine rhymes (hover/cover, Decembers/remembers), the second and fourth in masculine ones (grave/wave).
body: Each quatrain rhymes abab, with feminine (two-syllable) rhymes in the first and third lines of most stanzas ('hover / cover', 'Decembers / remembers'; the first stanza rhymes on the single syllable 'thee') and masculine rhymes in the second and fourth ('grave / wave'). The lines often open with a heavy stress ('Cold in the earth'), giving a falling, dirge-like rhythm. The insistent caesura of the opening line, with its dash, imitates a voice breaking off. The regular stanzas give the poem a restraint that contains its intense feeling, a quality critics frequently praise.

anchor: Have I forgot, my only Love
title: The question of forgetting
short: The speaker asks whether she has forgotten her love; the whole poem answers that she has not, though she has had to suppress her memory.
body: The rhetorical question in the first stanza sets out the poem's subject: fidelity to the dead after many years. In the fourth stanza she asks forgiveness 'if I forget thee', and by the end she admits she must deliberately refrain from remembering, since memory would destroy her. The poem thus moves from guilt at forgetting to the stoical decision not to remember too much. 'Forgot' is an older past participle (modern 'forgotten').

title: 'Time's all-severing wave'
short: Time is a sea or river that cuts every tie; the image of a tide recurs in 'the world's tide' (l. 14).
body: The image recalls the classical rivers of the underworld that separate the living from the dead, and Gondal's island geography, where lovers are parted by seas. The compound 'all-severing' is a poetic coinage in a Miltonic manner. The wave image returns as the 'world's tide' that bears the speaker along, so that time and the world are both currents moving her away from the grave.

title: 'that northern shore'
short: In the Gondal saga the grave lies in a distant northern land; in the published version, the moorland setting evokes the Brontës' Yorkshire.
body: The speaker's thoughts are imagined as birds that rest their wings over the grave, 'Over the mountains'. In Gondal terms the northern shore is the place where Julius was buried, far from Rosina; without the names, readers have naturally associated the 'heath and fern-leaves' and 'brown hills' with the Haworth moors. The landscape links this poem to Wuthering Heights (1847), where Heathcliff mourns Catherine buried at the moor's edge.

title: 'fifteen wild Decembers'
short: Fifteen winters have passed since the death, the span fixed by the Gondal story.
body: Julius Brenzaida had been dead for fifteen years at the date of the poem's dramatic situation. The figure is synecdoche: winters stand for years, and their thaw 'into spring' measures time's passage over the grave. The parallel with Heathcliff, who opens Catherine's grave eighteen years after her death, is often noted. The adjective 'wild' gives the weather some of the passion the speaker restrains in herself.

title: Other desires
short: The speaker admits that other hopes and desires have claimed her, but insists they cannot wrong the dead love.
body: The fourth stanza is the poem's admission of guilt and its plea for forgiveness. 'Beset' (l. 15) means surround and press upon, as besiegers do; the new hopes 'obscure' the old love but do not betray it. In the Gondal story the claims of 'the world' belong to Rosina's later life; in the published poem the line describes any survivor's return to life.

title: 'No later light'
short: She declares that no second love has replaced the first: all her happiness came from the dead beloved and lies buried with him.
body: The fifth stanza is a vow of exclusive fidelity built from anaphora ('No later light ... No second morn', 'All my life's bliss ... All my life's bliss'). The light-and-morning imagery makes the dead lover the sun of the speaker's world. The repeated line places all bliss first in 'thy dear life' and then 'in the grave', compressing the history of the relationship into two lines.

title: Existence without joy
short: When even despair had failed, she learned that existence can be valued and sustained without joy: the poem's stoic core.
body: This stanza is central to readings of the poem. Having passed beyond 'golden dreams' and even beyond despair (which was 'powerless to destroy' her), the speaker discovers that life can be 'cherished, / Strengthened, and fed' without happiness. Some critics take it as hard-won stoicism, a choice to live; others read it as a near-heroic resignation that keeps feeling alive only by denying it. The language of feeding and strengthening treats the soul as a body kept alive on a meagre diet.

title: 'Weaned my young soul'
short: She withdrew her soul from its yearning as a child is weaned from the breast, an image of painful self-discipline.
body: The metaphor of weaning (compare Psalm 131:2, 'my soul is even as a weaned child') presents the separation as necessary for growth but painful. She also 'denied' her soul's 'burning wish to hasten / Down to that tomb', that is, the desire to die and join the beloved. The phrase 'already more than mine' means that the tomb belongs more to her than her own life does, since her heart is buried there. The stanza's rhymes include the half-rhyme 'passion / hasten'.

title: The closing refusal
short: She dares not let herself remember fully: once she drank that 'divinest anguish', she could never return to the 'empty world'.
body: The final stanza explains the poem's apparent forgetting: it is a defence. Oxymorons ('rapturous pain', 'divinest anguish') name the grief she fears to indulge, because it is too sweet. The 'empty world' to which she must return is the world of the living. F. R. Leavis is often cited as ranking 'Cold in the earth' very high among the nineteenth-century poems in the Oxford Book of English Verse, while also treating it as an imaginative exercise rather than personal confession (the exact source of the remark should be checked before it is quoted); others value it as a profound study of mourning.
